title: Chapter 111 – Zhou's Ledger
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Jian does not take the paper.

He closes Ruyan's fingers over it, gently, one at a time, as if folding the hand of a child, and he says, "Keep it. Do not sign it. Do not show it to anyone. If the Court meets and I am still eleventh, we will talk about it again."

"That is not an answer."

"It is the only one I can afford." He stands. The step is cold under his boots. "Ruyan, how long would it take you to read the payroll of a department you have never been inside?"

Her dark eyes narrow. "That depends on the department. And whether the payroll is kept honestly."

"The Hall of Weights."

For the length of a breath she does not move. Then she lets out a small, hard laugh, and tucks the paper back into her sleeve.

"Three days," she says. "Two, if the clerks are lazy. And they are always lazy."

* * *

The Court sits on the first of the month, in the long pale room above the Hall of Law, and it takes the petition in under four minutes.

Jian stands at the foot of the table in the gray of a Foundation disciple with his hands folded before him. He has written the petition himself, three paragraphs, in the plainest language he can find. He asks for nothing but a second measure. He does not say the Mirror is false. He says only that his Qi has been read as Foundation Early by a device that read him as Foundation Middle the season before, that a hundred people watched the sky open over his head, and that a second reading would settle it.

Five seats face him. Cheng Yun sits on the left, in the black of a Court magistrate, with his stylus laid across a roll. Qin Hao is in the center, narrow and still. Two Elders from the Hall of Law flank them, and on the far right, with his hands tucked into his sleeves, sits a man Jian has seen only at a distance: Elder Zhou of the Treasury, sixty years old, round-faced and mild, with the soft clean hands of a man who has never held anything heavier than a seal.

Zhou smiles at him. It is a very kind smile.

"The Hall of Weights," says Zhou, in a warm slow voice, "is of course eager to assist. The Mirror is old, and old instruments drift. A re-measure would do no harm." He turns his palms up. "I would only ask that it be done in the proper place, with the proper witnesses, and that the disciple not be permitted to prepare."

"Prepare how?" asks Cheng Yun.

"Pills. Stimulants. The Hall has seen such things." Zhou sighs. "A young man under pressure will do many things."

Jian keeps his face still. He does not look at Qin Hao.

"The petition is granted," says Qin Hao, in his dry voice. "The re-measure will be held at noon, on the ninth, before this Court. The disciple will be examined by two of our own healers beforehand. Elder Zhou may send a witness."

"I will send two," says Zhou pleasantly.

The stylus scratches. The roll is sealed. And as Jian bows and turns to go, he sees, for just an instant, the kind round face tilt toward the window, and the soft hand come up to smooth a sleeve, and nothing in it at all.

He is not afraid, he thinks. Because he already knows how it ends.

* * *

The Garden Hall is full of lamplight when he reaches it, and loud with the sounds of a clan that has stopped being small.

Wenyuan has taken the long room off the east cloister for his study. Charts cover the walls: birth rolls, stall rolls, the muster of the trained and the untrained, the roster of the school. In the center of the floor, on a mat, sit Qinghe with a ledger on her knee and Hu with soot to the elbow, arguing in the low rapid voices of people who have argued before. Yue, fifteen now, sits cross-legged at the end with a brush, copying something. Beside the brazier a small boy of five is asleep on a pile of cloaks, and nobody has moved him.

"Two hundred and thirty-one," says Wenyuan, when Jian has bowed to the room and found a place. "As of this morning. Eleven new from the Tan side, six from the Zhao muster, and a birth." He allows himself one dry look. "We are running out of rooms."

"Then build."

"We are building. Hu has promised the east wing by the end of the month, and Qinghe has promised herself that the roof will not leak." Wenyuan sets down his brush. "We are also being watched. There is a man at the end of the lane who sells chestnuts and has no chestnuts. Dai was here twice this week. She did not ask for a ward. She only counted the beds."

"I know."

"You know the ranking."

"I know the ranking." He tells them, in four sentences, because they will hear it from Feng in the morning in forty. Hu swears, quietly and with variety. Qinghe's pen stops. Yue, at the end of the room, lifts her head, and her gray eyes are very clear and very old.

"They are taking the stair," she says.

"They are trying."

"Then we make another door." She says it without heat, as if reading a line from a sutra. "A clan of two hundred can dig a tunnel."

Hu barks a laugh. Wenyuan does not. He looks at the girl for a long moment, and then at Jian, and then at the sleeping boy by the brazier.

"We are not yet strong enough to be reckless," he says at last. "But we are strong enough to be patient. Tell us what you need, and we will find it."

"Time," says Jian. "And quiet."

"Those," says Qinghe, setting her ledger aside, "we can do."

* * *

The ledger comes on the fifth night.

Ruyan brings it to the old Pill Hall annex, where Bai keeps a stove and a bad cot and a pot of something that smells of burnt plums. She comes in alone, wrapped to the chin in a gray traveling cloak, and sets a flat parcel on the table with the care of a woman putting down a sleeping baby.

"I did not steal it," she says. "I want that understood. A Tan house clerk copied it in the Treasury annex, openly, under the pretext of an audit for the Spring Tithe. Three hundred and eleven pages. I read all of them."

"And?"

"And the Hall of Weights is run like a clock." She unwraps the parcel. The paper inside is thick, creamy, and slightly yellow. "Salaries. Rations. Repairs to the Mirror, by a firm in the lower town. Stipends for visiting examiners. All of it sound. All of it signed." She flips to a page near the end and lays her finger on a line. "Except this."

Jian bends over it.

It is a list of small payments, twelve in all, one for each of the last twelve months. Special Services. Cloud Peak Annex. The sums are not large. Forty silver in the first month, fifty in the third, then a steady sixty. They are signed Zhou Mengyan, with an Elder's seal in red.

"The Annex is not a department," says Ruyan. "I checked. It is a storehouse. Eight rooms on the north terrace. Nothing is kept there but old furniture."

"Who receives the money?"

"There is no receiving name. The entry says to the bearer." She turns the page. "But I followed the coin. Each payment was drawn from the Hall's contingency purse and carried to the Treasury window on the same morning by the same courier. A girl of sixteen from a paper stall in the lower town. I found the stall." Her voice flattens. "The paper is plum bark."

Bai, stirring his pot with a long spoon, grunts. "Plum bark. That's the House's paper."

"It is."

"You'd be surprised how many people don't know that." The old Elder chews on something, and spits a pit into the fire. "Zhou is a careful man. I trained him, forty years ago. Not as an alchemist. As a bookkeeper. He's never done anything he couldn't write down."

"He wrote this down," says Jian.

"He wrote it down in a book that isn't supposed to be read." Bai squints at him over the spoon. "Which means he's more frightened than he looks."

Jian studies the page. Twelve months. Twelve payments. The first was made three weeks after the charter was signed.

He has the Door in Autumn. He has twenty-two points left and a Seal that is straining, and he could use two of them now, to look at the ink, to see whether the signature was laid by the hand that wrote the sums. It would take a moment. It would also tell him nothing the page does not already say.

Sixty silver a month, he thinks. That is what it costs to buy a Mirror.

It is so small. It is a number a clerk would hide under a sum for lamp oil. The Registry does not buy officials with gold; it buys them with a salary. It finds the man who is already honest, already careful, already trusted, and gives him a second small income to place beside the first, and asks nothing in return but that he forget what the second one is for. In a year the man cannot stop. In two he cannot explain.

"What do you want to do with it?" asks Ruyan.

"Nothing yet."

"Nothing?"

"If I put this on the Court table, Zhou will say it is a gift fund. He will say the courier is a charity runner. He will say the Annex holds the Hall's winter stores." Jian shakes his head. "He will be believed, because he is Zhou. And the girl at the paper stall will be gone by morning."

Bai chuckles. It is not a pleasant sound. "He's learning."

"I have had good teachers."

"You've had terrible ones. They all died." The old Elder lays his spoon down. "Take the book. Keep it where it can't be found. And boy, don't go near the Annex."

* * *

He goes to the Annex three nights later.

He does not go inside. He is not that foolish. He goes at dusk with a bundle of dried herbs under his arm, in the guise of a Pill Hall errand boy, and he walks the length of the north terrace slowly, as a man does who is lost.

It is a long low building of gray stone with eight doors. The doors are shut. The windows are shuttered. A single lantern burns at the end of the terrace, and under it, on a stool, sits a guard in the plain brown of a Cloud Peak porter, whittling a stick.

Jian passes him without a glance. He turns the corner at the end of the row. And there, in the lee of the wall where the wind does not reach, he lets his eyes go soft and opens the Door in Autumn.

The cost is two points. He has twenty-two.

The stone sharpens. The shutters, the latches, the dust in the cracks all stand out like carvings. And across the whole face of the building, drawn like a net over the doors and windows and roof, hangs a faint web of silver-gray: not a single thread but hundreds, laid in a neat dense lattice, each one fine as spider silk.

A ward, he thinks. Not a Sect ward. A Registry one.

He follows the web along the wall. It is strongest at the fourth door. There it thickens, knotted and layered, and at its center, small as a seed, glows a cold point of light.

He knows that light. He has seen it at the base of his own skull, under the Door's sight, on the night he first found the binding mark. It is a locator. It has been placed here to say: someone is watching this room.

He does not touch it. He closes the Door and walks on, and the cold in his stomach does not leave until he is back among the lamps of the lower terrace.

Eight rooms of old furniture, he thinks. And one of them is wired like a vault.

* * *

The Court's two healers come to him the evening before the re-measure.

They are quiet, courteous, middle-aged men in the gray-and-white of the Hall of Law, and they examine him in a bare room with a lamp and a stone couch, as they might examine a goat for the market. One takes his pulse at the wrist and the throat. The other lays a cool palm on his sternum and sends a thread of Qi through him, slowly, from the heart to the base.

Jian lies still. He lets the thread go where it wishes.

It is the old danger. A healer can read what a Mirror cannot: the shape of a vessel, the roughness of a meridian, the places where Qi has been forced. His own are scarred. The left arm especially, where the Spring Vein runs gray and thin beneath the skin, is a map of everything he has done in seven years. He has hidden it by habit, long sleeves and good lies. He can do nothing now but breathe.

The healer's palm slides down. It stops over the left forearm.

"Old injury," says the man, mildly.

"A fall, as a boy."

"A bad one."

"Yes."

"The channel has healed oddly." The thread in his arm turns, lingering, and for a heartbeat Jian's stomach clenches. Then the healer shrugs. "It will trouble you in cold weather. Keep it warm. Nothing in it to bear on the examination." He rises. "You are in excellent health for a man of your standing, Gate Bearer. Better than the Mirror will credit."

"Thank you."

"Do not thank me. I have been told to report any stimulants, tonics, or arts of concealment. There are none." The healer smiles faintly. "There is, however, a remarkable stillness. I should not like to be the one who tried to unsettle you."

When they have gone he lies for a long time on the stone couch with his hand over his eyes.

They could not see it, he thinks. But they looked.

And a single worry stays with him, small and cold, as the lamp gutters low: the healers had been sent by the Court, and the Court was not the only body that wished to know what the left arm was.

* * *

Qin Hao finds him in the corridor outside the room.

Qin Hao does not stop walking. He falls in at Jian's shoulder, narrow and still in the black of his office, and speaks to the air in front of him.

"A tied vote is still a vote."

"Ye told me you had said so."

"Ye tells a good deal." There is the faintest crease at the corner of the old man's mouth. "The Court is not the Sect. I can order a re-measure, and I did. I cannot order the Hall of Weights to be honest. The Rule is a cage, not a leash. It stops men from doing certain things. It does not make them do others."

"And Elder Zhou?"

"Is a man I have known for forty years." Qin Hao's voice does not change. "I should have preferred to be wrong about him."

They walk on past a window and a stairwell and a long blank wall of painted screens. The old man speaks again only when they have reached the head of the great stair.

"Whatever you decide to do, do it in writing. On a Court form. With a witness. I cannot protect what I cannot see."

"Yes, Elder."

"And Lin Jian." The old man stops at last, and turns, and his dark eyes are quite steady. "If a note comes. If someone offers you a quicker road. Remember that I have never once been asked to make a quick decision that I was glad I made."

He goes down the stair. The black hem vanishes round the turn.

* * *

The re-measure is held on the ninth, at noon.

It is done in the Hall of Law, in the long pale room above the courtyard, with the sun pouring through the high windows and the Mirror carried up from the Hall of Weights on a litter by four porters. The bronze disc is placed on a low plinth in the center of the floor. Round it, in a half circle of chairs, sit the Court, the healers, two of Zhou's clerks, and thirty of the Silver Leaf ranked above him, who have come to watch.

Jian takes off his boots. He steps onto the plate.

The disc hums.

This time he does not close his eyes. He keeps them open, wide and steady, fixed on the rings of light as they rise in the air, and he does not use the Door. He has made a decision, and the decision costs him nothing but patience: he will let the Mirror speak, and he will see what it says.

White. Red. Blue.

Qi, says the reading clerk, in a high thin voice. Foundation Middle. Step six.

A rustle runs through the room.

Body. Foundation Early. Step five.

Soul. Foundation Early. Step five.

It is correct. All three. He feels, rather than sees, the faces turn toward him: the watching Silver Leaf, the pale healers, Cheng Yun with his stylus suddenly still. He feels Qin Hao's eyes on his back like a hand.

Zhou's two clerks look at each other. One of them clears his throat.

"The Mirror is accurate," says the elder of the two, carefully. "The earlier reading was in error. The Hall of Weights regrets the inconvenience."

"It does not regret it," says Cheng Yun. "It records it. There is a difference." The magistrate rolls the paper. "The petition is satisfied. The disciple's ranking will be recalculated on the corrected figures."

Jian bows. He steps off the plate.

That was easy, he thinks. And the cold wire in his gut pulls tight.

* * *

It was too easy, and he understands why before the bell has stopped ringing.

The recalculated ranking is posted at dusk, and his name is not on it. Not eleventh. Not first. He searches the board from the top and cannot find it. At the bottom, in the margin, in a small clean hand, a clerk has written:

LIN JIAN: RANKING SUSPENDED. Pending review of examination irregularities (Formation, day two).

"The note I left on the stone," he says aloud, quietly.

"The note you left on the stone," agrees Ye, coming up beside him with her stick. She has been waiting for him at the foot of the board, he realizes, for an hour. "Brilliant. Honest. A clear statement of what you saw, under your own token. And Zhou's clerks have read it, and found it troubling."

"They are claiming I accused the Hall of tampering."

"They are claiming you submitted a false examination paper. That you invented a foreign filament in order to excuse a poor result." Her voice is dry as leaves. "It will be heard before the Arbiter in the spring. Until then, your ranking is held. And Article forty-four, as amended, says that a Gate Bearer without a ranking has no standing."

He closes his eyes.

"The Mirror was corrected," he says.

"The Mirror was corrected. It was never the point." She leans on her stick. "They did not need you to lose. They needed you to act. To raise a flag. To put your seal on a paper that says I saw something the Hall did not. Now there is a charge against you that cannot be answered without proof you cannot give."

"The Door."

"The Door."

He opens his eyes. The board is a pale blur. The disciples are drifting away in little knots, talking in low voices, glancing at him and away. He sees Ruyan at the far end of the hall, standing very straight, her hands folded in her sleeves. She does not come over.

"What does it cost?" he asks.

"The stair." Ye does not soften it. "For the season. Perhaps for two, if the Arbiter is slow. You may still enter the Dock on sufferance, by my signature, for the Sutra Hall's work. But the register will not accept a suspended hand. The bench will not open. And the Spring Vein—"

"Is dormant in the cold anyway."

"Yes." She meets his eyes. "I am sorry. I thought we had four months. We have four hours."

* * *

Ruyan catches him at the foot of the Hall steps before he has gone ten paces. She has crossed the whole length of the hall to do it, and her breath is short.

"You did not warn me it would be this," she says.

"I did not know."

"The paper is still in my sleeve." Her mouth is a thin line. "It would not help now. Would it? Your name is not on the board at all. There is nothing to cede."

"No."

"Then what do I do with it?"

"Keep it." He looks at her ink-stained fingers, at the jade pin, at the weary angry girl who tore a page from her family's book and handed it to a stranger. "Keep reading, Ruyan. Sixty silver a month. Find me every other place in the Sect where that figure appears. Do not go alone. Do not put it in writing until I say."

She nods once, sharply, as she would to a client.

"Then I will need a bigger pretext," she says, and walks away into the dusk.

He walks down to the Dock alone that night, because he must see it for himself.

The passage is dark. The air smells of stone and old lamp-oil. At the bottom, the plain door waits in its frame, and he lays his palm against the lock as he has done a hundred times, and nothing happens.

Then, very slowly, a line of pale text rises on the metal.

```
OPERATOR ARK-7 :: ACCESS QUERY
SECT STANDING: SUSPENDED (EXTERNAL)
DOOR IS SEALED BY SECT AUTHORITY, NOT BY ARK.
OPERATOR OVERRIDE AVAILABLE.
COST: 40 CE. SEAL STRAIN: SEVERE. THE OVERRIDE WILL BE VISIBLE TO EVERY WARD ON THIS HILL.
```

He reads it three times.

Forty points. He has twenty-two, and the Spring Vein sleeps under the frost, and the Pill Hall's night labor pays two a night to a cap of six a week. Even if he could pay, the override would light the hill like a beacon. Every Registry ward on the terrace would feel the door open. The locator in his skull would answer.

He takes his hand from the metal.

The text fades. The door stays shut. He stands in the dark for a long time, listening to the faint, patient hum of the thing on the other side, the bench, the register, the lamp that has been waiting for him for seven years. He feels, for the first time since the Gate, something like loneliness.

It does not hold it against me, he thinks. It is only a door.

He turns and climbs the stair.

At the top, in the thin gray light of the first frost, a figure is waiting. Small. Straight. In the plain brown of an apprentice. He holds a lantern in one hand and a folded paper in the other, and her face, when the light touches it, is the face of Zhao Hui.

He is thirteen, and he should be in bed. He holds out the paper without a word.

He takes it. The paper is plum bark, cream-colored and rough. In the corner is a black square.

Inside, in a clerk's even hand, there is a single line.

The Court is slow. The House is not. Come to the Annex, alone, on the night of the new moon, and the Gate Bearer's suspension will be lifted by morning.

Hui's voice is very small in the cold.

"It was left at the school," she says. "On my desk. Under my brush."
